name: Teach loose-lead walking
blurb: The most commonly failed dog skill, because pulling is self-rewarding — every pull gets the dog closer to where it wants to go. Fixing it takes consistency more than technique.
gear: A well-fitted harness with a front clip, or a flat collar
A 2 m lead, never an extendable one for training
steps: Understand the mechanism: pulling works, so it continues. The fix is making pulling never work.
Start indoors and in the garden, rewarding the dog for being beside you before you ever go out.
Stop dead the instant the lead goes tight, and only move when it slackens. Every single time, without exception.
Reward heavily in the position you want, feeding at your leg so that spot becomes valuable.
Use the environment as the reward: sniffing and greeting happen only on a loose lead.
Accept that progress means shorter, slower walks at first, and use a long line in safe open spaces for exercise meanwhile.
tips: Any inconsistency resets the training. If pulling works on one walk in ten, the dog will keep trying.
Extendable leads teach the dog that pulling extends their range. They actively train pulling.
proof: A relaxed 20-minute walk on a slack lead past normal distractions.
